description: Understanding ECG waveforms, intervals, and their clinical significance
overview: This module covers the detailed analysis of ECG waveforms including P waves, QRS complexes, T waves, and the measurement of important intervals.
objectives: Identify and analyze P wave characteristics
Recognize normal and abnormal T waves

slides.title: P Wave Analysis
slides.content: The P wave represents atrial depolarization. Normal characteristics include: duration <0.12s, amplitude <2.5mm, upright in leads I, II, aVF, V4-V6, and biphasic in V1. Abnormal P waves may indicate atrial enlargement or conduction abnormalities.

slides.title: QRS Complex
slides.content: QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization. Normal duration is <0.12s. Q wave should be <0.04s and <25% of R wave amplitude. Abnormal QRS may indicate bundle branch blocks, ventricular hypertrophy, or myocardial infarction.

quiz.question: What is the normal QRS duration?
quiz.explanation: Normal QRS duration is less than 0.12 seconds (3 small squares).

slides.title: T Wave and ST Segment
slides.content: T wave represents ventricular repolarization. ST segment should be isoelectric. ST elevation or depression indicates myocardial injury or ischemia. T wave inversion may indicate ischemia, electrolyte abnormalities, or normal variants.

quiz.question: What does ST elevation typically indicate?
quiz.explanation: ST elevation typically indicates myocardial injury, such as in acute myocardial infarction.

slides.title: PR and QT Intervals
slides.content: PR interval (0.12-0.20s) represents AV conduction time. QT interval varies with heart rate but should be <0.44s for men and <0.46s for women. Prolonged QT may lead to dangerous arrhythmias.

quiz.question: What is the normal PR interval range?
quiz.explanation: The normal PR interval is 0.12-0.20 seconds, representing atrioventricular conduction time.
